findings.headline: The Deficit on the Provision of Services was £11,818k in 2025/26, against £10,717k in 2024/25.
findings.detail: The paper states that the accounting cost in the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement can differ from the amount raised from taxation, which is why the accounting deficit sits alongside a management outturn that was £180k below budget.
findings.matters: A finance director reading the accounts needs to see the gap between the budget outturn and the accounting result, as it is the figure that moves the general reserves.
findings.figures: Deficit on the Provision of Services: £11,818k in 2025/26, £10,717k in 2024/25. Management outturn: £180k below budget.
findings.quote: (Surplus) or Deficit on the Provision of Services 126,963 (115,145) 11,818

findings.headline: Cash and cash equivalents fell from £12,940k to £6,006k, and the bank overdraft rose from £1k to £1,882k over 2025/26.
findings.detail: The balance sheet shows nil short-term and long-term borrowing at both dates. Long-term investments fell from £21,255k to £16,424k, and short-term investments fell from £36,292k to £33,681k.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director watches the movement from cash to overdraft closely, since it shows short-term liquidity pressure in the year.
findings.figures: Cash and cash equivalents: £12,940k at 31 March 2025, £6,006k at 31 March 2026. Bank overdraft: £1k, then £1,882k. Long-term investments: £21,255k to £16,424k. Short-term investments: £36,292k to £33,681k.
findings.quote: Cash and Cash Equivalents – Bank Overdraft 19 (1,882)

findings.headline: East Lindsey was awarded £1.164m of government funding for significantly affected councils in 2025/26 and expects a similar level in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says the government announced additional funding to support councils significantly affected by the levies it describes earlier in the section, which is not included in this extract. The council expects a similar level of funding in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Funding for councils hit by levies is a cost offset that other councils facing the same levies will want to compare.
findings.figures: Government funding: £1.164m awarded in 2025/26, similar level expected in 2026/27.
findings.quote: East Lindsey awarded £1.164m in 2025/26, and the Council expects a similar level of funding in 2026/27.

findings.headline: In September 2026 the government asked all bodies to cease work on Local Government Reorganisation implementation pending a review.
findings.detail: The paper records that in July 2026 the government decided to create two new unitary authorities in Lincolnshire, with shadow elections in 2027 and new authorities expected from April 2028. In September 2026 that decision was put under review. The council says the implications for it 'remains uncertain'.
findings.matters: A council's medium-term plan, reserves and debt position depend on whether it continues in its current form, so lenders and finance directors need to track the reorganisation timetable.
findings.figures: None given beyond the timetable: shadow elections 2027, new authorities expected April 2028.
findings.quote: all bodies have been asked to cease work on LGR implementation until that review is complete

findings.headline: The NNDR Collection Fund showed a £0.374m deficit at 31 March 2026, while the Council Tax Collection Fund showed a £1.019m surplus.
findings.detail: The NNDR deficit is shared between the council, Lincolnshire County Council and the Government in proportion to each party's share. The Council Tax surplus is shared between the council, Lincolnshire County Council and Lincolnshire Police and Crime Commissioner in proportion to precepts.
findings.matters: Collection Fund balances affect the following year's budget, so other councils will want to see how their own deficits and surpluses are being carried.
findings.figures: NNDR Collection Fund: £0.374m deficit. Council Tax Collection Fund: £1.019m surplus.
findings.quote: The balance on the NNDR Collection Fund at 31 March 2026 showed a £0.374m deficit.

findings.headline: Paper says reserves provide "a sufficient buffer"; proposes £10m from useable reserves for ELIF 2
findings.detail: The paper proposes allocating a further £10m from useable reserves to a new 'ELIF 2' investment scheme, following the success it reports for 'East Lindsey Investment Fund 1'. The paper also says the council is diversifying its income and exploring additional financial strategies.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare how much this council is drawing on reserves against its own stated limit, and the proposed £10m commitment shows the scale of planned use.
findings.figures: Proposed ELIF 2 allocation: £10m from useable reserves.
findings.quote: While our reserves currently provide a sufficient buffer to meet ongoing pressures and finance transformation projects, relying solely on these reserves is unsustainable over the long term.

findings.headline: Specific and general reserves fell by £325k over 2025/26, from £39,009k to £38,684k, with the Economic Growth Reserve drawn down by £3,388k.
findings.detail: The Economic Growth Reserve went from £5,511k to £2,642k. The Corporate Priorities (Investment) Reserve rose from £11,327k to £11,855k, and a new Waste Transformation Reserve of £1,956k was established.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how fast economic-growth reserves are being drawn down against the same types of scheme.
findings.figures: Total specific and general reserves: £39,009k at 1 April 2025, £38,684k at 31 March 2026, £325k net decrease. Economic Growth Reserve: £5,511k opening, £3,388k used, £2,642k closing. Corporate Priorities (Investment) Reserve: £11,327k to £11,855k. Waste Transformation Reserve: £1,956k at year end.
findings.quote: The net decrease in specific and general reserves and balances for 2025/26 was £0.325m.

findings.headline: Total Towns Fund capital spend was £8,973k against £14,611k approved in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Within the Towns Fund, Skegness Railway Station spent £216k against £1,688k, and Mablethorpe Sandilands spent £428k against £1,755k. Skegness Learning Campus was close to budget at £4,296k against £4,319k.
findings.matters: Externally funded regeneration programmes with large slippage are a point of comparison for other councils delivering Towns Fund schemes.
findings.figures: Total Towns Fund: £14,611k approved, £8,973k actual, £5,638k variance. Skegness Railway Station: £1,688k budget, £216k actual. Mablethorpe Sandilands: £1,755k budget, £428k actual.
findings.quote: Total Towns Fund 14,611 8,973 (5,638)

findings.headline: The 2025/26 capital outturn was £24,777k against an approved budget of £45,771k, a £20,994k variance.
findings.detail: The paper states that the unspent capital budget is needed for commitments to complete programmes still in progress. Largest variances include Sustainable Warmth at £2,076k against £5,469k, CDF – Pier Transformation at £192k against £4,000k, and Public Conveniences at £92k against £1,650k.
findings.matters: Large capital slippage is a common issue for councils, and the carry-forward commitments show how far the programme is pushed into future years.
findings.figures: Capital programme: £45,771k approved budget, £24,777k actual, £20,994k variance. Sustainable Warmth: £5,469k budget, £2,076k actual. CDF – Pier Transformation: £4,000k budget, £192k actual. Public Conveniences: £1,650k budget, £92k actual.
findings.quote: Grand Total – All Projects 45,771 24,777 (20,994)

findings.headline: Investment income was £2,988k against a £2,149k budget, £839k above it.
findings.detail: The outturn table shows the investment income variance as favourable. The narrative puts investment interest at £3.3m (4% of income), a different figure from the table, which the paper does not reconcile in this extract. The Investment Volatility Reserve is described as holding funds to mitigate a downturn in investment income.
findings.matters: A large share of the outturn depends on investment returns, so a finance director here or elsewhere will want to know how far the surplus relies on that income.
findings.figures: Investment income: £2,149k budget, £2,988k outturn, £839k above budget. Narrative: £3.3m investment interest, 4% of income.
findings.quote: Investment Income (2,149) (2,988) (839)

findings.headline: Directorate net costs were £29,703k against a £29,246k revised budget, a £457k overspend, with Planning & Strategic Infrastructure £604k under budget.
findings.detail: Within directorates, Planning & Strategic Infrastructure was £388k against £992k, Neighbourhoods was £7,444k against £7,296k, and Regulatory was £1,529k against £1,441k. Corporate Priorities and the efficiencies line make up the balance.
findings.matters: A finance director sees the same pressures in the service lines, and the offsetting underspends show where the overall position was held.
findings.figures: Directorates net costs: £29,246k revised budget, £29,703k outturn, £457k overspend. Planning & Strategic Infrastructure: £992k budget, £388k outturn, £604k underspend. Neighbourhoods: £7,296k budget, £7,444k outturn, £148k overspend. Regulatory: £1,441k budget, £1,529k outturn, £88k overspend.
findings.quote: Directorates – Net Costs 29,246 29,703 457

findings.headline: The revised 2025/26 budget carried a £1,128k efficiencies requirement, and the outturn table shows no figure against it.
findings.detail: The efficiencies requirement appears as a £(1,128)k revised budget line with an outturn shown as a dash and a £1,128k variance. The paper's table does not explain how the requirement was treated.
findings.matters: A savings target showing no outturn is a question other councils tracking efficiency programmes will want answered.
findings.figures: Efficiencies requirement: £1,128k revised budget (shown as (1,128)k), no outturn figure, £1,128k variance.
findings.quote: Efficiencies Requirement (1,128) - 1,128

findings.headline: The 2025/26 General Fund outturn was £180k below budget, and the budget surplus was transferred to reserves.
findings.detail: The management accounts show net budget costs of £35,812k against a £35,992k revised budget. Funding came in £763k above budget and that amount was transferred to earmarked reserves, leaving a total budget surplus of £180k.
findings.matters: A finance director here or at a peer council can compare how a balanced management outturn sits alongside the accounting deficit in the next theme.
findings.figures: General Fund budget net costs: £35,992k revised budget, £35,812k outturn, £180k underspend. Funding: £763k above budget. Transfer to earmarked reserves: £763k.
findings.quote: The full year outturn delivered spend of £180k below budget. The budget surplus has been transferred to reserves.

findings.headline: Local Government Ombudsman findings, counting upheld decisions in the financial year, rose from 1 in 2024-25 to 3 in 2025-26
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit's opinion stayed at Adequate in both years. KPMG notes the Ombudsman findings figures but did not identify a significant weakness in governance from them.
findings.matters: A rise in upheld Ombudsman decisions is a governance signal that other councils will compare against their own complaint outcomes.
findings.figures: Local Government Ombudsman upheld findings: 3 in 2025-26; 1 in 2024-25
findings.quote: Local Government Ombudsman findings

findings.headline: Strategic risk for the long-term balancing of the budget is scored 12 (High) and held at its target score, with the Council tolerating the risk
findings.detail: The paper reports the 'Budget' strategic risk at a score of 12 (High) in both the quarter two and quarter four risk reports, at its target score. It describes this as the Council tolerating the risk.
findings.matters: A council that formally tolerates a high-scoring budget risk, while also missing its savings target, is a position a finance director and a lender will want to see stated plainly.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (High) in quarter two and quarter four reports; at target score
findings.quote: The risk is at the target risk score which means the Council is ‘tolerating’ the risk.

findings.headline: Government withdrew its October 2026 Local Government Reorganisation decision, with a structured review outcome expected by early 2027
findings.detail: The paper traces a July 2026 decision to create two new unitary authorities in Lincolnshire, a September 2026 government review that required bodies to cease implementation work, and an October 2026 announcement withdrawing that decision. It says the outcome of the structured review is expected by early 2027.
findings.matters: Reorganisation affects the council's future structure, debt and financial planning, and other councils in the same reorganisation process will track the same timetable.
findings.figures: Review outcome expected early 2027; implementation originally expected from 1 April 2028
findings.quote: In October 2026 the government announced the above decision has been withdrawn and a structured approach to review will now take place and an outcome is expected by early 2027.

findings.headline: Council reports no year-end borrowings and year-end cash of £6.006m, down from £12.940m
findings.detail: The key financial metrics table shows gross debt and year-end borrowings both at nil, with the capital financing requirement at £20.802m. Year-end cash fell by £6.934m across the year.
findings.matters: A council with no external borrowing, but a capital financing requirement of £20.802m, is a position a lender or peer finance director will read against its cash balances and future capital plans.
findings.figures: Year-end borrowings nil; gross debt nil; capital financing requirement £20.802m; year-end cash £6.006m (2024-25: £12.940m)
findings.quote: Year-end cash position 6,006 12,940

findings.headline: Interim s151 officer who left in November 2025 did not complete a declaration of interest, and the 2025/26 PSPS service level agreement was not agreed amid s151 officer turnover
findings.detail: The paper reports that 5 of 10 Councillor declarations tested did not include interests recorded at Companies House, with a compensating control by PSPS. It also says the 2025/26 SLA with the finance-service company was not updated, mainly due to the turnover of the s151 officer. The 2024/25 SLA remained in place and an update for 2026/27 is being agreed.
findings.matters: Turnover in the s151 role, and an unsigned service agreement for the outsourced finance function, are the kind of leadership and control gaps that other councils with shared finance services will want to check.
findings.figures: 5 of 10 Councillor declarations tested incomplete; 10 senior officer declarations tested with no inconsistencies; 2024/25 SLA remained in place
findings.quote: mainly due to the turnover of the s151 officer during the year

findings.headline: KPMG reports no significant risks identified to date across financial sustainability, governance, and improvement of economy, efficiency and effectiveness
findings.detail: The value-for-money summary table records no significant risks identified and no actual significant weakness identified for each of the three criteria, with a stable direction of travel. KPMG notes that its findings may change when its work is complete.
findings.matters: A clean value-for-money assessment alongside open audit points is useful context for any council or lender reading the Auditor's Annual Report.
findings.figures: Three criteria: financial sustainability, governance, improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness; direction of travel unchanged
findings.quote: No significant risks identified to date.

findings.headline: KPMG has not yet reached conclusions on the 2025-26 financial statements or Whole of Government Accounts, with value-for-money work described as substantially complete
findings.detail: The report was issued before the financial statements audit was finished in order to meet the 30 November deadline. KPMG says its work on the statements and other information is substantially complete but without conclusions, and that it cannot yet confirm completion of the Whole of Government Accounts procedures. It also says it may still exercise other powers.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, needs to know the audit opinion is still pending before relying on the 2025/26 accounts.
findings.figures: Report deadline 30 November; financial statements conclusion outstanding; Whole of Government Accounts conclusion outstanding
findings.quote: whilst our work is substantially complete, we have not reached our conclusions in respect of these areas.

findings.headline: A 2023/24 performance improvement observation on a formal efficiency programme remains open, with the follow-up in October 2025 confirming it was not implemented
findings.detail: The observation, raised as medium risk in the 2023/24 audit, asked for a formal efficiency programme. KPMG confirmed in October 2025 that it had not been implemented. The paper says it remains open because there is still no formal programme to identify, RAG-rate and monitor efficiencies.
findings.matters: A formal efficiency programme is the mechanism that would have tracked the £1.1m shortfall; an open recommendation on it is directly relevant to any council running an efficiency target.
findings.figures: Medium-risk observation raised in 2023/24 audit; not implemented at October 2025 follow-up
findings.quote: we have concluded that this performance improvement recommendation remains as there is not a formal programme in place to effectively identify, RAG rate and/or monitor efficiencies.

findings.headline: Internal Audit gives Limited Assurance on the identification and monitoring of savings, and reports no documented escalation process for savings not on schedule
findings.detail: Internal Audit's second review of savings identification and monitoring, reported in March 2026, found that a governance process for 2026/27 savings had been introduced, but that no formal escalation process existed for savings not on schedule. A first review in the same area could not be completed because there were insufficient controls to test.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance on savings monitoring, alongside an untestable first review, is a control weakness that other councils facing savings targets will recognise.
findings.figures: Head of Internal Audit opinion: Adequate (2025-26 and 2024-25); one Limited Assurance report; one review with insufficient controls to test
findings.quote: a Limited Assurance review was reported in relation to the identification and monitoring of savings.

findings.headline: Internal Drainage Board levies rose 42% since 2021/22 to £5.39m in 2025/26, with £1.2m of Government grant funding offsetting part of the cost
findings.detail: The paper describes the IDB levy as a continuing cost pressure, with a budgeted cost of £5.3m in 2025/26, a 1.5% increase on 2024/25. The Council is liaising with the Internal Drainage Boards to limit future increases.
findings.matters: A levy that rises faster than the council's own budget, and depends on in-year grant to offset, is a cost pressure that other councils in drainage areas will face and that lenders will weigh against the council's income position.
findings.figures: £5.39m IDB levy in 2025/26 (budgeted £5.3m); 42% rise since 2021/22; £1.2m Government grant; 1.5% budgeted increase on 2024/25
findings.quote: Internal Drainage Board levies remain a significant financial pressure, increasing by 42% since 2021/22 to £5.39m in 2025/26.

findings.headline: General Fund earmarked reserves fell from £37.19m to £36.86m in 2025/26, after a £325k transfer to the General Fund balance
findings.detail: The paper states the General Fund balance was £1.82m at 31 March 2026. It reports a £325k decrease in the balance, and then says the transfer from earmarked reserves left the General Fund total unchanged from 31 March 2025. Usable reserves are shown as £51.578m, down from £62.809m.
findings.matters: A transfer from earmarked reserves to general fund reserves, and a fall in usable reserves from £62.809m to £51.578m, both bear on the council's capacity to absorb future pressures.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £1.82m; earmarked reserves £37.19m to £36.86m; £325k transfer; usable reserves £51.578m (2024-25: £62.809m)
findings.quote: General Fund earmarked reserves decreased from £37.19m to £36.86m during the year, a net decrease of £325k (due to the transfer from earmarked to general fund reserve).

findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by £20.9m against its 2025/26 budget, with actual capital additions to Property, Plant and Equipment of £6.741m
findings.detail: The year-end capital position is reported as a £20.9m underspend. The statement of financial position table shows a planned capital budget of £45.771m and actual capital additions of £6.741m, against £19.471m in 2024-25. At 30 September 2025, the paper had forecast a £4.4m underspend.
findings.matters: A large gap between planned and delivered capital spend affects borrowing needs and the timing of schemes, which matters to lenders and to councils planning similar programmes.
findings.figures: £20.9m capital underspend; £45.771m planned capital budget; £6.741m actual capital additions (2024-25: £19.471m); £4.4m forecast underspend at 30 September 2025
findings.quote: The year-end position confirmed the Council had an underspend of £20.9m against its capital budget for the year.

findings.headline: Council reports a balanced 2026/27 budget without additional efficiency savings, and no efficiency target in its Medium-Term Financial Plan through 2030/31
findings.detail: The paper says the 2026/27 budget was balanced without additional efficiency savings, consistent with the Medium-Term Financial Plan, which includes no efficiency target up to and including 2030/31. Earlier in the paper, the Council is described as having to find efficiencies to balance the 2025/26 budget.
findings.matters: A medium-term plan with no efficiency target is a specific planning position that a finance director, or a lender assessing future budget gaps, would want to compare against peers.
findings.figures: 2026/27 balanced budget; no efficiency target to 2030/31; 2025/26 budgeted gross expenditure £107.8m
findings.quote: This is consistent in the Medium-Term Financial Plan where there is no efficiency target included up to and including 2030/31.

findings.headline: Of the £2.29m 2025/26 efficiency target, £1.2m was met through Internal Drainage Board funding and £1.1m was not delivered by year-end
findings.detail: The efficiency requirement combined a £1.58m IDB Funding Requirement and a £0.7m Annual Budget Efficiency requirement. The IDB element was met by Government funding announced in-year, and the paper says none of the remaining £1.1m was achieved.
findings.matters: It shows a savings target being met by an external grant rather than by council-identified savings, which matters to any council relying on in-year funding to close a gap.
findings.figures: £2.29m efficiency target; £1.2m met through IDB funding; £1.1m not delivered; £1.58m IDB Funding Requirement; £0.7m Annual Budget Efficiency requirement; IDB pressure 65% of the total efficiency requirement
findings.quote: Of the Council’s £2.29m efficiency target for 2025/26, £1.2m was met through this funding.

findings.headline: East Lindsey reports a £180k underspend against its 2025/26 general fund budget, with £839k of additional investment income offsetting an undelivered efficiency target
findings.detail: The paper reports that none of the remaining £1.1m of planned efficiency savings was delivered, and that favourable variances elsewhere, including £839k of additional investment income, produced an overall underspend of £180k. The paper also describes the quarter two forecast as both a £418k deficit and a £418k surplus.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can see how an unmet savings target was absorbed by income and other variances rather than reserves, and that the year-end position depended on the quarter two forecast being read consistently.
findings.figures: £180k underspend; £839k additional investment income; £1.1m efficiency savings not delivered; £418k quarter two forecast (described as both deficit and surplus)
findings.quote: The remaining £1.1m of planned efficiencies was not delivered by year-end, although favourable budget variances, including £839k of additional investment income, contributed to an overall underspend of £180k.

findings.headline: Combined net asset value of the property funds fell by £363,612 in the first half of 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper reports a decrease in the combined net asset values of all property funds in the first half of the year. It states that the fair value movement is charged to the revenue account and reversed through the MIRS to the capital adjustment account, so there is no bottom-line impact.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare how a fall in property fund values is treated through the revenue account and the capital adjustment account with their own accounting for similar holdings.
findings.figures: Decrease in combined net asset values £363,612 (first half of 2026/27); combined property fund net asset value £15,770,909 before the M&G distribution adjustment
findings.quote: has been a decrease of £363,612.

findings.headline: AEW Property Fund shareholders agreed a managed winddown at an extraordinary meeting on 31 July 2026
findings.detail: The paper reports that the AEW fund's proposed managed winddown was approved following a shareholder vote. Sale receipts are expected in the current year and will be used to pay the MRP charge. The paper says the winddown is likely to take more than two years to maximise sale receipts.
findings.matters: A council with a unfinanced property fund holding that is now winding down has to plan MRP and cash receipts around a multi-year exit, which is a common issue for councils holding similar funds.
findings.figures: AEW UK Core Property Fund net asset value £3,749,276 against a purchase cost of £4,800,000; winddown expected to take more than two years
findings.quote: a vote from shareholders this proposal was agreed.

findings.headline: M&G UK Property Fund has paid £4,949,182 in distributions against an original investment of £4.8m, a current gain of £149,182
findings.detail: The paper says the M&G fund is liquidating its assets and that fund valuation is falling as repayments are made. The distributions will be used to fund a corresponding MRP charge, because the original purchase was unfinanced capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Liquidation distributions that are applied to MRP show how a council is using a property fund exit to meet a statutory charge, which a peer council could copy.
findings.figures: Distributions paid £4,949,182; original investment £4.8m; current gain £149,182
findings.quote: £4,949,182 as of 30 September 2026 resulting in a current gain of £149,182.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure of £8.555m at Quarter 2 against a revised budget of £37.633m, with an estimated outturn of £36.267m
findings.detail: The capital table shows the approved budget of £39.666m reduced to a latest revised budget of £37.633m, and an estimated outturn of £36.267m. The borrowing requirement is revised from £7.829m to an estimated £7.555m.
findings.matters: The gap between Quarter 2 spend and the full-year budget, and the revised borrowing requirement, show how far the capital programme is running behind its original timetable.
findings.figures: Approved budget £39.666m; latest revised budget £37.633m; Quarter 2 actual £8.555m; estimated outturn £36.267m; borrowing requirement estimated outturn £7.555m

findings.headline: Council has no external borrowing apart from leases and has used £20.953m of cash flow funds in lieu of borrowing
findings.detail: The paper states that the council's capital financing requirement is £20.953m and that it has used cash flow funds in place of borrowing. It describes this as prudent and cost-effective in current conditions, but says it will need ongoing monitoring if gilt yields stay elevated, particularly at 25 to 50 years.
findings.matters: A council running on internal borrowing with no external debt is a different credit and funding position from one that has borrowed, and the paper ties the position to yields at the long end of the curve.
findings.figures: Capital financing requirement £20.953m; cash flow funds used in lieu of borrowing £20.953m; Operational Boundary for borrowing £32,000k
findings.quote: had utilised £20.953m of cash flow funds in lieu of borrowing as at 30 September

findings.headline: Discounts on early repayment of borrowing are £418,356 at Quarter 2 and £834,425 in the forecast outturn
findings.detail: The net treasury position table records early repayment discounts allocated in the year, with the same amount at Quarter 2 and in the forecast outturn. The paper does not identify the loans concerned.
findings.matters: Early repayment discounts are a direct sign of debt being retired ahead of maturity, which affects the council's borrowing profile and what a lender is exposed to.
findings.figures: Quarter 2 discount £418,356; forecast outturn discount £834,425 (both in £)

findings.headline: Net treasury position forecast at a favourable variance of £1,230,844 against the 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The paper reports a Quarter 2 favourable variance of £961,560 and a forecast outturn favourable variance of £1,230,844. It attributes the higher investment income to market interest rates above the budgeted return and to higher investment balances from slippage in the capital programme.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how a forecast investment income variance of this size arises from rate movements and capital slippage rather than from new income sources.
findings.figures: Forecast outturn favourable variance £1,230,844; Quarter 2 favourable variance £961,560; forecast net investment income £2,316,176 against an annual budget of £1,375,200
findings.quote: and the forecast outturn is a favourable variance of £1,230,844.

findings.headline: Value for money commentary is to be issued ahead of the 30 November publication deadline
findings.detail: KPMG's value for money commentary, reported in the Auditor's Annual Report for 2025/26, will be provided before the body publishes it on its website. The paper gives no findings in this section.
findings.matters: The 30 November publication date for value for money reporting is a deadline every council must meet, so the timing is useful to other finance teams.
findings.figures: 30 November publication deadline
findings.quote: This will be provided in advance of the 30 November deadline for the body to publish on their website.

findings.headline: The audit is "substantially complete", with litigation and claims, cash flow statement and management representation letter among the outstanding matters
findings.detail: The paper lists outstanding matters including litigation and claims, rebuilding-assurance testing for capital receipts, finalisation of land and buildings estimate work, the cash flow statement and completion procedures. It states the audit report will be finalised and signed after these.
findings.matters: The list of open items shows what remains before the final opinion, which finance directors can use to judge the timing of their own closedown and audit milestones.
findings.quote: Our audit is substantially complete

findings.headline: KPMG reports management override of controls testing as "satisfactory"
findings.detail: The paper lists management override of controls as a standard significant risk with no specific additional risk identified. It reports no exceptions in the testing of accounting policies. It identifies 12 high-risk journals, none indicative of fraud.
findings.matters: The absence of fraud indicators from journal testing is a positive point for the Council's control environment that peer councils can compare against.
findings.figures: 12 high-risk journals and other adjustments tested
findings.quote: Testing in this area was satisfactory.

findings.headline: The defined benefit obligation valuation is moved from a significant risk to an other audit risk, citing reduced estimation uncertainty after the 2025 triennial valuation
findings.detail: KPMG reassessed the post-retirement benefit obligation during planning. It cites stable methodology and assumptions, no significant exceptions in prior-year testing, and no significant expected movements in discount and inflation rates. The paper also notes the new triennial valuation may still correct the obligation and asset valuations this year.
findings.matters: A downgrade in the pension liability's audit risk, while the triennial valuation could still correct it, is a point other councils with LGPS liabilities would want to compare.
findings.quote: we have reclassified the LGPS Defined Benefit Obligation (DBO) valuation from a significant risk to an other audit risk

findings.headline: Uncorrected audit misstatements include £0.3m against the deficit for the year (3.2%) and £0.3m against total reserves (0.2%)
findings.detail: The table lists uncorrected misstatements in the deficit for the year, total assets and total reserves. Each is shown as -£0.3m. The deficit effect is 3.2% and the reserves effect is 0.2%. The paper states that all disclosure misstatements were corrected by management.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements of this size against the deficit and reserves show how the auditor's materiality applies to the Council's headline outturn figures.
findings.figures: Deficit for the year -£0.3m (3.2%); total assets -£0.3m (0.1%); total reserves -£0.3m (0.2%)
findings.quote: Total reserves -£0.3 0.2%

findings.headline: Control deficiencies for the year are reported as 0 significant and 4 other, with 9 prior-year control deficiencies remediated
findings.detail: KPMG reports no significant control deficiencies and four other control deficiencies in the current year. Nine control deficiencies from the prior year are recorded as remediated. The General Ledger does not enforce segregation of duties, which KPMG reports as making journal controls ineffective.
findings.matters: A count of nine remediated deficiencies alongside four open ones is the measure a peer council would use to compare its own control environment with East Lindsey's.
findings.figures: 0 significant control deficiencies; 4 other control deficiencies; 9 prior year control deficiencies remediated
findings.quote: Prior year control deficiencies remediated

findings.headline: KPMG reports the management review control over the land and buildings valuation as "ineffective", with no counter-signatory to the valuer's report
findings.detail: The internal valuer is the only qualified surveyor used for a significant portion of other land and buildings. Review is carried out by finance staff with no counter-signatory. KPMG reports the design and implementation of the management review control as ineffective, while noting management operates a control it is satisfied with.
findings.matters: A review control over a £57.99m valuation that the auditor reports as ineffective, with no second signatory, is a control gap a finance director would want to see closed.
findings.quote: Auditing standards require us to report that the design and implementation of the management review control relating to this area is ineffective in line with the ISA definition.

findings.headline: Other land and buildings subject to indexation total £57.99m, the first year of the rolling revaluation model, and are recorded as a significant audit risk
findings.detail: The Council adopted a rolling five-year revaluation model under the 2025/26 Code. Assets valued using depreciated replacement cost at 31 March 2026 total £25.08m. KPMG identifies a significant risk that indexed assets are misstated through index selection and asset categorisation.
findings.matters: Other councils adopting the same rolling model under the 2025/26 Code face the same first-year indexation and categorisation risk on their property balances.
findings.figures: £57.99m indexed other land and buildings; £25.08m other land and buildings valued using depreciated replacement cost
findings.quote: The total value of other land and buildings that were subject to indexation was £57.99m.

findings.headline: The 2024/25 audit report was disclaimed over usable and unusable reserves at 31 March 2025, which the paper cites as evidence KPMG could not obtain before the backstop
findings.detail: The paper restates the 2024/25 basis of disclaimer. KPMG was unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over usable and unusable reserves at 31 March 2025 for the Group and the Council. Comparative balances at 31 March 2024 were also affected.
findings.matters: Reserves are the basis of a council's financial resilience, so a finance director elsewhere will want to know that the reserves balance itself is what the auditor could not verify.
findings.quote: We were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the balance of usable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025

findings.headline: KPMG states it will issue a qualified opinion on the 2025/26 group accounts, citing its rebuilding-assurance work and the 31 January 2027 statutory backstop date
findings.detail: The paper says the audit report will be qualified because of the status of the rebuilding-assurance work, progress on the current-year audit and the backstop date. The basis of the qualification will be set out in the final report. The 2025/26 comparatives for income and expenditure and the balance sheet at 31 March 2025 are cited as areas where work could not be completed.
findings.matters: A finance director here or at another council needs to know that the 2025/26 opinion is expected to be qualified and that the backstop, not only the work done, is driving the outcome.
findings.figures: statutory backstop date 31 January 2027
findings.quote: we will be issuing a qualified opinion

findings.headline: The paper expects a reduction in Bank Rate over the remainder of the 2026/27 financial year.
findings.detail: The paper's economic outlook section gives the expected direction of interest rates for the second half of the year. The paper does not give a forecast size for the reduction.
findings.matters: A lower Bank Rate would reduce the investment income that has driven the favourable variance, so the forecast matters to councils with similar cash balances.
findings.figures: None given.
findings.quote: The expected direction of interest rates for the remainder of the financial year is a reduction in Bank Rate.

findings.headline: The M&G liquidation distribution included in the Quarter 2 figures will be used to finance a corresponding MRP charge.
findings.detail: The paper states that the M&G liquidation distribution is included in the net treasury variance and will be applied against a matching minimum revenue provision charge. The paper gives no amount for either figure.
findings.matters: Using a property fund distribution to fund a matching MRP charge is a specific accounting treatment a finance director may need to replicate or check.
findings.figures: None given.
findings.quote: The liquidation distribution from M&G which is included in these figures will be used to finance a corresponding MRP charge.

findings.headline: The combined rate achieved on all investments was 4.02% (Quarter 1 4.00%), with treasury investments at 4.32% (Quarter 1 4.34%) and property fund investments at 3.24% (Quarter 1 3.19%).
findings.detail: The paper reports the average returns by investment type for Quarter 2 alongside Quarter 1. Treasury investments fell slightly and property fund investments rose.
findings.matters: Comparing the split between treasury and property fund returns against the same quarter last year is a basis for assessing a portfolio's returns at other councils.
findings.figures: 4.02% (combined, Q2); 4.00% (combined, Q1); 4.32% (treasury investments, Q2); 4.34% (treasury investments, Q1); 3.24% (property fund, Q2); 3.19% (property fund, Q1)
findings.quote: The combined rate achieved on all investments was 4.02% (Q1 4.00%).

findings.headline: Investment income is above the original budget because market interest rates are higher than budgeted and capital programme slippage has increased balances available for investment.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the higher investment income to two causes: market rates above the 2026/27 budgeted return, and higher cash balances from slippage in the capital programme. The first cause is a market factor; the second is a timing effect on capital spending.
findings.matters: Capital slippage raising cash balances, and so investment income, is a pattern other finance officers can check against their own capital monitoring.
findings.figures: None given for the size of either effect.
findings.quote: balances available for investment being higher due to slippage in the capital programme

findings.headline: The net treasury position at Quarter 2 shows a favourable variance of £961,560, with a forecast outturn favourable variance of £1,230,844.
findings.detail: The paper reports the combined net treasury variance at Quarter 2 and the projected full-year outturn. It states that a liquidation distribution from M&G is included in these figures.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the size and direction of a mid-year treasury variance against their own budget monitoring.
findings.figures: £961,560 (Quarter 2 favourable variance); £1,230,844 (forecast outturn favourable variance)
findings.quote: At Quarter 2 the net treasury position shows a combined favourable variance of £961,560 and the forecast outturn is a favourable variance of £1,230,844.

findings.paper_title: ELDC A&G Committee - October 2026 Budget Setting 2027-28
findings.headline: The paper says the previous Local Government Reorganisation decision has been withdrawn and the proposals reconsidered, and that this uncertainty may require revisions to budget and Medium Term Financial Plan assumptions.
findings.detail: The paper lists the withdrawal of the previous reorganisation decision among the factors that may affect funding and cost assumptions. It states that the MTFP will be prepared without relying on unconfirmed LGR savings or implementation dates, and that LGR-related costs and funding will be monitored separately.
findings.matters: A council facing a possible change of structure and an unconfirmed timetable has to plan how long existing services, contracts and debt commitments will run, and other councils in the same position will be watching how that is handled.
findings.figures: None given in the paper. Dates cited: first draft MTFP 30 October 2026, Executive Board 9 December 2026, Full Council final budget 3 March 2027.
findings.quote: uncertainty following withdrawal of the previous Local Government Reorganisation decision and reconsideration of the proposals

findings.headline: Investment income forecast to outperform budget by £1.2m, heavily dependent on temporary rate environment
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £1.375m investment income but is forecasting £2.599m outturn—an outperformance of £1.224m. This is explicitly attributed to higher interest rates than budgeted (treasury investments yielding 4.34%, property funds 3.86%) and higher cash balances from slippage in the prior year's capital programme.
findings.matters: While the income boost improves the revenue account and cash position, it is vulnerable to reversal if the Bank of England cuts rates (currently at 3.75%) or if capital spending accelerates and depletes cash. The council's financial plan is dependent on temporary market conditions.
findings.figures: Budget £1,375,200; forecast outturn £2,599,084; favorable variance £1,223,884; treasury yield 4.34%, property yield 3.86%
findings.quote: The higher level of investment income achieved compared to the original budget is due to interest rates in the market being higher than the budgeted return for 2026/27 and balances available for investment being higher due to slippage in the 2025/26 capital programme.

findings.headline: No new borrowing anticipated despite £38.8m capital budget
findings.detail: The council expects to fund its 2026/27 capital programme entirely from existing resources without undertaking new long-term borrowing. This reflects strong cash generation and investment balances totalling £62.6m at end of Q1.
findings.matters: A local authority forecasting no borrowing need indicates sufficient liquidity and no external financing requirement, demonstrating financial resilience and that the council is managing within existing resources.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure budget £38.8m; investments held £62.6m at Q1; no temporary borrowing outstanding
findings.quote: It is anticipated that new long term borrowing will not be undertaken during this financial year.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage from 2025/26 has left higher cash balances available for investment than projected
findings.detail: The council achieved investment income of £503,706 in Q1 against a budget of £177,837, a favorable variance of £325,869. The council attributes this outperformance partly to higher interest rates and partly to 'balances available for investment being higher due to slippage in the capital programme from 2025/26'. The report does not specify the scale of the slippage, its underlying cause, or whether the capital spending is expected to be recovered.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage indicates planned capital expenditure did not proceed as scheduled, which may reflect resource constraints, procurement delays, or project delivery issues. Lenders need to understand whether capital plans are realistic and executable, as slippage affects future borrowing requirements and cash flow.
findings.figures: Q1 investment income £503,706 actual vs £177,837 budget
findings.quote: balances available for investment being higher due to slippage in the capital programme from 2025/26

findings.paper_title: V3 ELDC Audit Governance Annual Report 2025 26 - Reviewed KB
findings.headline: Risk management framework does not provide confidence that risks are managed consistently and effectively
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit concluded that while the risk management framework was in place and subject to regular review, 'current arrangements did not provide confidence that risks were managed consistently and effectively.' The Committee noted that improvement was required to strengthen risk management practices.
findings.matters: Consistent and effective risk management is essential to financial stability and service delivery. If the council cannot reliably identify and manage emerging risks, exposures may be missed that could impact the council's financial position or ability to meet obligations.
findings.figures: Assessment from Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025/26 presentation, June 2026
findings.quote: However, current arrangements did not provide confidence that risks were managed consistently and effectively; the proposed improvements would help to further strengthen its maturity and consistency.

findings.paper_title: V3 ELDC Audit Governance Annual Report 2025 26 - Reviewed KB
findings.headline: Internal audit identified Insufficient Controls relating to identification and monitoring of savings, described as 'extremely serious'
findings.detail: In September 2025, internal audit raised a finding of Insufficient Controls over the identification and monitoring of savings. The Audit and Governance Committee chairman described this as 'extremely serious' because there were not enough processes in place to determine whether this aspect of finances was being run well. The issue was repeated in Q4, indicating it remained a focus area throughout the year.
findings.matters: A lender requires confidence that a council can reliably track and implement savings plans, which are typically critical to maintaining financial stability. Insufficient controls over savings identification means the council cannot adequately verify that planned savings are being delivered.
findings.figures: Findings identified in Q1 and Q4 2025/26
findings.quote: Another challenge has been the audit finding in September of Insufficient Controls relating to the identification and monitoring of savings. This was an extremely serious matter, because internal audit identified that there weren't enough processes in place to be able to tell whether this aspect of finances was being run well or not.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Capital Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: External grant spend lagging: only 51% of approved external grant budget actually spent (£16.881m of £32.838m)
findings.detail: Large variance between approved external grant budget and actual cash drawn suggests either forecasting misalignment or genuine delays in grant-funded schemes reaching completion. This implies future-year borrowing or reserve draw-down to fund rephased schemes.
findings.matters: If rephased schemes draw forward in future years, external grants may not follow; council may need to finance gaps internally, affecting liquidity and leverage ratios.
findings.figures: External grants: £16.881m spend against £32.838m budget, £15.957m underspend
findings.quote: capital spend was £24.777m against a full year budget of £45.435m an underspend of £20.994m

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Capital Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: External co-funding sources reducing: Football Foundation grant no longer available for Sutton Colonnade; UKSPF ends 30 September 2026 with no further allocation
findings.detail: Loss of specific project funding (Football Foundation grant for Multi Use Games Area, which is now not progressing) and broader government decision to end UKSPF as of end-September 2026. The UKSPF only extends for six months more with no additional funding. This removes a regeneration funding source and forces scale-back of one project.
findings.matters: Loss of external co-funding increases reliance on council reserves or borrowing; end of UKSPF removes circa £531k–£538k annual spending authority. Affects pipeline of future regeneration projects.
findings.figures: UKSPF budget 2025/26 £1.069m, extended only to 30 September 2026
findings.quote: Multi Use Games Area no longer progressing, Football Foundation grant no longer available as a result of this.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Capital Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: Car park resurfacing delayed specifically due to oil price cost uncertainty
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies volatility in input costs as a factor preventing completion of capital works by year end. This signals cost inflation pressure on future tender returns and project viability.
findings.matters: Direct evidence of market-driven cost inflation affecting delivery timings; affects budget planning and feasibility of future schemes in similar categories.
findings.figures: Car parks: £103k spent of £404k budget
findings.quote: There have been some delays with completing car park resurfacing works before year end by the 31 March 2026. The reasons for this are due to other workload within the Team and uncertainties with potential price increases due to the current oil crisis.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Capital Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: Capital programme spent £24.777m of £45.435m budget, with £17.369m of schemes rephased into future years
findings.detail: The council significantly underspent its capital budget, delivering only 54% of planned capital expenditure. Major regeneration schemes are substantially behind: Pier Transformation spent £192k of £4m (4.8%), Railway Station £216k of £1.688m (12.8%), and Public Conveniences £92k of £1.65m (5.6%). The council intends to rephase the shortfall rather than cancel schemes.
findings.matters: Capital underspend of this magnitude signals delivery risk on major projects; rephasing affects future borrowing demand, cash flow profiles, and the council's ability to meet strategic investment targets.
findings.figures: £24.777m actual spend, £45.435m budget, £20.994m underspend, £17.369m rephased
findings.quote: existing capital schemes totalling £17.369m of the £20.994m need to be rephased into future years

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX B ELDC Q4 Strategic Risks 260701
findings.headline: New Local Plan must commence by 31 December 2026 or government intervention risk applies
findings.detail: The council must begin a new Local Plan under government regulations that came into effect March 2026. The deadline for commencement is 31 December 2026. Failure carries risk of government intervention and loss of local planning control, with knock-on effects for the council's ability to shape development-led revenue and regeneration.
findings.matters: Government intervention in planning directly constrains the council's control over future development strategy and tax-base growth
findings.figures: Target deadline 31/12/2026; current risk High (12) reducing to Medium (6) once plan commences
findings.quote: Timeline now established for new plan - commencement by end of 2026

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX B ELDC Q4 Strategic Risks 260701
findings.headline: Council-owned Invest East Lindsey company solvency depends on pending income-split approval to avoid insolvency
findings.detail: The council owns Invest East Lindsey. The company's solvency depends on approval of an income-split arrangement. If that approval does not proceed, the company may become insolvent, with consequences including operational cessation, job losses, and disruption to ongoing projects. Currently Low (4) risk but contingent on a specific decision.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of all material liabilities including council-owned entities; this represents a specific decision point with solvency consequences for a council subsidiary
findings.figures: Risk score Low (4) assuming income-split approval; escalates if approval fails
findings.quote: If the income split is not approved, the company may face financial difficulties, potentially leading to insolvency. Insolvency could result in the cessation of operations, loss of jobs, and significant disruption to ongoing projects.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX B ELDC Q4 Strategic Risks 260701
findings.headline: Environment Act waste service changes impose operational costs without guaranteed ongoing funding
findings.detail: The Environment Act 2021 requires the council to change waste service delivery. While initial New Burdens funding was received, the council explicitly states it has no certainty about ongoing annual revenue funding to cover the operational cost increase. Current risk score is High (16); target date for mitigation was 30 June 2026, now passed.
findings.matters: This is an unfunded legislative mandate creating recurring cost pressure on the budget with no solution yet in place
findings.figures: Current risk High (16), Target Medium (9); ongoing New Burdens funding unknown
findings.quote: although some New Burdens has been made available information is not provided on the ongoing New Burgdens revenue funding to meet the additional cost of service delivery

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Revenue Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: Invest EL loans of £3.49m outstanding with unknown performance trajectory
findings.detail: The council has issued five loans to Invest EL totalling £3.49m (down from £3.69m after a £200k repayment). The council received £148k interest during the year. There is no information in this paper about the underlying company's performance, business plan, or likelihood of full repayment. This is material concentration risk in a single vehicle.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether Invest EL can service and repay these loans. The interest return (£148k on £3.49m = 4.2%) appears low for a development company, and the council has no information presented on performance or prospects.
findings.figures: Invest EL loans: £3.49m outstanding; interest received: £148k during year
findings.quote: In addition to the treasury investments the Council has issued five loans to Invest EL which totalled £3.69m... leaving a balance of £3.49m on 31 March 2026. Interest payments of £148k have also been received during the financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Revenue Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: Council Tax collection improved to 95.51% and Business Rates to 97.69%, though environment remains challenging due to cost of living crisis
findings.detail: Council Tax collection improved to 95.51% (from 95.47% prior year). Business Rates collection improved to 97.69% (from 97.05%). However, the paper explicitly states collection 'remain challenging in 2025/26 as a result of the ongoing cost of living crisis' and notes the council continues to set bad debt provisions 'prudently'. This suggests management expects further deterioration ahead.
findings.matters: Trend is currently favorable but the council's own language indicates expectation of pressure. A deteriorating collection environment is a forward-looking risk to revenue.
findings.figures: Council Tax collection: 95.51% (vs 95.47% prior year); Business Rates collection: 97.69% (vs 97.05% prior year)
findings.quote: Collection and recovery remain challenging in 2025/26 as a result of the ongoing cost of living crisis. In recognition, we continue to remain prudent in setting the bad debt provision in this area.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Revenue Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: Neighbourhoods service overspend of £148k driven by agency staffing for sickness and leave cover, plus vehicle costs
findings.detail: The Neighbourhoods directorate (waste, street cleaning, fleet) overspent by £148k. The paper cites agency and overtime costs for sickness and annual leave cover, vehicle running costs, fleet maintenance and insurance, plus bin purchases (purple lid bin replacement and increased skip usage). These are structural pressures, not one-off, and the paper gives no indication the council has addressed the root cause.
findings.matters: A recurring £150k annual overspend on a core service suggests either the budget is set too tight or the service is structurally pressured. Waste collection cannot be easily cut; this will return.
findings.figures: Neighbourhoods variance: +£148k overspend against £7.296m budget
findings.quote: Overspends on employee costs primarily linked to agency/overtime premium for sickness, annual leave and bank holiday cover. Combined with overspends in Vehicle costs associated with running costs, Fleet Maintenance and Insurance. Further overspends on bin purchases primarily due to a need to replace purple lidded bins and increased skip usage.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Revenue Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: Investment income of £2.881m includes £263k in non-recurring asset sale proceeds; budget was £2.149m
findings.detail: The council budgeted £2.149m in investment income and achieved £2.881m. However, £263k came from M&G property fund asset sales (liquidation proceeds). Strip that out and recurring income is £2.618m, still above the £2.128m budget net of fees. But the council is calling this a recurring £2.881m position. When the M&G fund is exhausted, income will drop significantly.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assume next year will deliver £2.881m in investment income. Stripping out asset sales, the council is generating around £2.6m from core investments, which is still above budget but declining.
findings.figures: Budget: £2.149m; Outturn: £2.881m; M&G asset sale proceeds: £263k
findings.quote: the budget for the year for treasury investment income net of property fund management fees was £2.128m and the actual was £2.881m giving a surplus of £753k. These figures exclude the M&G property fund asset sale distributions of £263k which has been used to finance the required Minimum Revenue Provision

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Revenue Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: Property fund portfolio down £3.1m in fair value; Federated Hermes fund has been liquidated at a loss
findings.detail: Between 2016-2019 the council invested in five capital property funds. The Federated Hermes revenue fund was merged and the council received £3.791m against an original cost of £4m (£209k loss). The M&G fund is liquidating and shows only £326k fair value against original £4m cost. The remaining four funds are now worth £16.1m against a purchase cost of £19.2m. During 2025/26 alone, the portfolio lost £777k in value. These are not paper losses—the council is realizing them through forced sales.
findings.matters: The council's investment reserves are being depleted through illiquid property fund positions. Liquidity is constrained and losses are accelerating as funds liquidate. This limits the council's ability to respond to shocks.
findings.figures: M&G: £4m original cost, £326k fair value; Federated Hermes: £4m cost, £3.791m received; Four remaining funds: £19.2m original cost, £16.1m fair value (£3.1m shortfall); Year loss: £777k
findings.quote: The M&G UK Property fund is liquidating its assets and therefore their fund valuation is reducing as repayments are made... leaving a book value of £141k outstanding. The fair value of the fund was £326k on 31 March 2026. As of 31 March 2026, the fair value of the remaining four funds was £16.1m which was £3.1m below the purchase cost.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - ELDC Outturn 25.26 Finance Revenue Report - EB 260701
findings.headline: Planning fee income spike of £883k is non-recurring and will not repeat
findings.detail: The council exceeded its budget for planning application fees by £883k due to high-value applications in a single year. It transferred £496k of this windfall into a newly created Planning Reserve, meaning the base budget is still £883k short of actual recurring need if income normalizes. Next year's budget should reflect this.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's finances depend on one-off wins. If next year brings normal-value applications, income will fall £883k short.
findings.figures: Planning Application fee income exceeded budget by £883k; £496k transferred to Planning Reserve
findings.quote: Planning Application fee income exceeded budget by £883k due to a number of high value planning applications received and processed during the financial year. As a direct result of this £496k (referenced in table 2b) has been transferred into the Planning Reserve

findings.headline: Council exceeded its £2.292m efficiency savings target for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council set an efficiency target of £2.292m for 2025/26. Given the final outturn showing a £180k overall underspend on the General Fund, the paper concludes that this savings target has been exceeded.
findings.matters: Demonstrating delivery of planned savings shows the council can implement cost controls and maintain financial discipline when required
findings.figures: £2.292m efficiency target exceeded; £180k final underspend achieved
findings.quote: An efficiency target of £2.292m was included in the 2025/26 budget. Saving opportunities were monitored throughout the year and in light of the outturn position showing an underspend of £180k it can be concluded that the savings target has been exceeded

findings.headline: Council's property fund investments lost £777k in value during the year
findings.detail: Property fund valuations declined by £777k net of distributions during 2025/26. The council holds property fund investments across six funds alongside loans to Invest EL.
findings.matters: Material investment losses indicate the council's portfolio is exposed to property market volatility and affect the quality and value of reserves available to manage future pressures
findings.figures: £777k reduction in property fund valuations
findings.quote: Property Fund valuations reduced during the year to 31 March 2026 by £777k net of M&G distributions

findings.headline: Capital programme spending fell nearly 46% short of budget, requiring rephasing of schemes into future years
findings.detail: The council budgeted £45.771m for capital expenditure in 2025/26 but only spent £24.777m, leaving a shortfall of £20.994m. The Executive Board is asked to approve rephasing of these underspent capital schemes into future financial years.
findings.matters: A capital underspend of this magnitude suggests capacity or delivery constraints that affect the council's ability to execute planned investments and may indicate project delays
findings.figures: £20.994m underspend on £45.771m budget (45.8% underspent)
findings.quote: As of 31 March 2026, capital expenditure totalled £24.777m against a full year budget of £45.771m an underspend of £20.994m

findings.headline: Interest rate environment shifted from falling rates to rising inflation concerns; market pricing rate increases to 4.0–4.25% from 3.75% by start of 2026/27.
findings.detail: The report documents three 0.25% Bank Rate cuts during 2025/26, but notes initial expectations for significant rate reductions across the curve did not materialise. By late March 2026, the outbreak of the Middle East conflict and rising energy costs triggered a sharp reassessment: the 10-year gilt yield rose from 4.23% in late February to 4.92% by end of March. Market expectations shifted to pricing in rate increases rather than cuts, with the report noting inflation could breach 4.5% later in 2026.
findings.matters: The abrupt reversal of rate expectations has direct implications for the council's borrowing costs if external funding becomes necessary. Any future capital scheme or deficit funding would occur at substantially higher cost than the rates available during 2025/26.
findings.figures: Bank Rate: 4.50% to 3.75% through 2025/26; end-March PWLB rates (1/5/10/25/50-year): 5.04% / 5.28% / 5.72% / 6.29% / 6.08%; market pricing rate increases; expected CPI: above 4.5% in late 2026
findings.quote: At the start of April 2026, the market expected Bank Rate to increase over the coming months to 4% or 4.25%, from 3.75%, whilst all parts of the curve have also risen substantially through March... UK inflation is likely to increase to over 4% in the coming months as oil prices, for example, remain close to $100 per barrel.

findings.headline: Council maintains zero external borrowing by using internal cash reserves, a strategy dependent on investment returns exceeding borrowing costs.
findings.detail: The council deliberately chose not to take external borrowing in 2025/26, instead funding its £20.8m capital financing requirement from reserves. Short-term borrowing for cash flow purposes was undertaken and repaid within the year, incurring £23,723 in interest costs. The strategy is described as prudent because near-term investment rates (averaging 4.50%) were higher than forward market rates for longer-term borrowing.
findings.matters: While described as prudent during a period of falling rates, this strategy actively consumes reserves and depends on investment returns remaining superior to borrowing costs. The paper's discussion of rising inflation and potential rate increases suggests this assumption may become fragile.
findings.figures: External borrowing at 31 March 2026: £0k; short-term borrowing interest: £23,723; capital financing requirement: £20,802k; average investment return: 4.50%
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Authority maintained an under-borrowed position. This meant that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), was not fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow was used as an interim measure. This strategy was prudent as near-term investment rates have generally been lower than medium to long-term borrowing costs.

findings.headline: Usable reserves fell by £11.2m to £51.6m, driven by £11m reduction in capital grants unapplied.
findings.detail: Total balance sheet resources declined from £62.8m to £51.6m. The most significant movement was capital grants unapplied, which fell from £22.3m to £11.3m, indicating the council deployed over £11m in grant funding during the year. Earmarked reserves also fell marginally from £37.2m to £36.9m. This pattern shows active depletion of liquid resources.
findings.matters: A reduction in available grants and usable reserves restricts the council's financial flexibility. For a lender, declining liquid resources signal either planned drawdown of accumulated grants (positive if deployed to capital schemes) or forced depletion due to revenue pressures.
findings.figures: Total resources: £62,809k (2024/25) to £51,578k (2025/26); capital grants unapplied: £22,332k to £11,347k; earmarked reserves: £37,187k to £36,862k

findings.headline: Capital expenditure delivered at 56% of budget: £25.1m actual versus £44.6m approved, a £19.5m shortfall.
findings.detail: The council budgeted £44.6m for capital expenditure but spent only £25.1m, leaving a programme underspend of 44%. This material variance persists despite an approved capital strategy and suggests either overly optimistic planning, programme delivery challenges, or a deliberate scaling back of capital activity not reflected in budget documents.
findings.matters: Persistent capital programme underspend raises questions about planning credibility and execution capability. For lenders, this indicates either risk that planned capital schemes may not deliver, or that the council is deliberately constraining its capital ambitions.

findings.headline: Property fund investments show cumulative unrealised losses of £2.9m, with £716,433 loss in 2025/26 alone.
findings.detail: The council holds £19.3m in capital property funds. During 2025/26, four of five funds posted losses, the largest being Schroder UK Real Estate (£483k loss) and AEW UK Core (£370k loss). In August 2025, the Federated Hermes fund was sold following a merger, resulting in a principal impairment of £208,981. The cumulative unrealised loss across all property funds now totals £2.9m since purchase.
findings.matters: A material erosion of the council's capital reserves through investment losses directly weakens its financial position and constrains future flexibility. For a lender, persistent losses on property fund investments signal either timing risk in the capital strategy or structural underperformance.
findings.figures: Property funds purchase cost: £19,339,742; cumulative net unrealised losses: £2,915,355; 2025/26 unrealised loss: £716,433; Federated Hermes principal impairment: £208,981
findings.quote: The total unrealised losses on the capital property funds during 2025/26 was £716,433. The total cumulative net unrealised losses on the capital property funds now stands at £2,915,355.

findings.headline: Capital receipts are minimal (£57k only) across the entire six-year period, with no planned asset disposals in years 2-6.
findings.detail: The only capital receipt shown is £57k in 2025/26. This is exceptionally low for a capital programme of this scale and suggests either no planned asset sales beyond 2025/26, or that the council has already disposed of most surplus assets.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a traditional source of capital funding. Absence of planned receipts limits financing options and may indicate the council has limited assets available to sell, or has chosen not to rely on disposals—either of which has implications for future capital funding flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital Receipts: (57) in 2025/26; zero in all subsequent years.

findings.headline: Nearly 70% of the capital programme is funded by external grants, many from time-limited schemes that end by 2027/28.
findings.detail: External grants total £60.3m of £89.1m (68%). Most grant funding is concentrated in 2025/26 (£32.7m). Major schemes—Towns Fund (Skegness Learning Campus £4.3m, Foreshore £1.4m, Town Centre Transformation £957k), LUF (Spilsby Sessions House £5.3m, Alford Manor House £2.7m), and UKSPF (£1.1m)—depend on government grant rounds that may not be confirmed or could slip.
findings.matters: Grant-dependent capital programmes create funding risk. If any major grant is not confirmed, delayed, or cancelled, the council faces either a gap in planned investment or forced reliance on higher internal borrowing or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: External Grants: (32,660) in 2025/26, declining to (2,531) by 2030/31. Total: (60,297).

findings.headline: Other reserves drawn down by £7.4m in 2025/26 alone, with ongoing draws until reserves fall to £140k/year by year 4.
findings.detail: The council is drawing £7,393k from other reserves in the current year (2025/26), then £3,476k in 2026/27, declining to £140k in years 4-5. This is on top of £2,793k from capital reserves in 2025/26. Reserve depletion accelerates in year 1 and early year 2 before stabilising.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion in the early years creates risk: if spending overruns occur or grants are delayed, the council has limited financial headroom. A finance director would need to confirm that remaining reserves are adequate for operational contingencies.

findings.headline: Capital spending drops from £44.4m in 2025/26 to £3.2m by 2030/31, with most decline after grant-funded schemes end.
findings.detail: Spending falls 93% over five years. The sharp decline correlates with the end of time-limited grant schemes (Towns Fund, UKSPF, LUF) which together represent £22.2m of the £89.1m total. By 2027/28, spending has already fallen to £9.5m; by 2029-30 it is £5.3m.
findings.matters: This pattern suggests the council's capital capacity in later years depends on external grants. If grant funding is delayed, cancelled, or unfunded elements of the programme are deferred, the council may lack planned capital investment or face pressure to rely further on internal borrowing.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing rises steeply to £7.1m in 2026-27, the highest single year across the forecast period.
findings.detail: The council shifts from £1.4m internal borrowing in 2025/26 to £7.1m in 2026-27, then declining in later years. Internal Borrowing is the largest funding source after external grants for that year. The paper shows no repayment schedule or revenue budget statement to support this borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director would need to verify that revenue budget can support £7.1m+ repayment, and would want to see a repayment strategy that does not depend on grants or reserves that may not materialise.

findings.headline: New £10m discretionary investment fund (ELIF 2) launched during funding uncertainty, with £4m drawn from Corporate Priorities Reserve in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council is allocating £10m for East Lindsey Investment Fund 2, a discretionary investment scheme funded from the Corporate Priorities Reserve. The 2026/27 revenue contribution is £4.029m. This discretionary spend is occurring while the council faces significant medium-term funding uncertainty and a potential 15%+ funding reduction after 2028/29.
findings.matters: Deploying reserve balances for discretionary investment, rather than retaining them for operational buffer or to mitigate funding shortfalls, reduces financial flexibility at a time when it is most needed. Success depends on these investments generating sufficient returns.

findings.headline: Capital programme expanded to £89m with internal borrowing jumping to £7.1m (397% increase), suggesting declining grant funding or expanded capital ambitions.

This represents borrowing of internal cash reserves to fund capital investment rather than using external grants or capital receipts. The increase suggests either capital investment ambitions have expanded or that grant funding for capital schemes has declined.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing depletes cash reserves and reduces the council's financial flexibility. Large increases in internal borrowing year-on-year, especially during a period of funding uncertainty, can constrain future options.

findings.headline: Internal Drainage Board levies rising structurally with no council control, consuming 5.7% of spending and described as 'embedded levy having an impact every year that passes'.
findings.detail: IDB levies increased £59k in 2026/27 and are forecast to rise every year through the MTFS. The Lindsey Marsh Drainage Board, which accounts for 78% of total IDB costs, has increased 39.10% since 2021/22 (from £3.057m to £4.252m). The council is lobbying government but explicitly states it cannot control these costs. The risk register rates IDB as HIGH likelihood, HIGH impact.
findings.matters: IDB levies are a cost the council must pay but cannot control or influence through efficiency. As an embedded cost increasing faster than general inflation, they consume an increasing share of the budget year-on-year and reduce financial flexibility.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Budget Setting Report and Associated Financial Strategies - 2026 27-2030 31 - Council 260304
findings.headline: Transitional funding support ends after 2028/29, with Fair Funding Assessment reduction of 15%+ anticipated from 2029/30 with no identified mitigation.
findings.detail: The council receives 95% protection on income through 2028/29, after which this protection expires. The council explicitly anticipates a Fair Funding Assessment reduction of more than 15% from 2029/30 onwards. No compensating funding or savings plan has been identified to address this funding cliff. The risk register lists this as HIGH likelihood, HIGH impact, with mitigating action only to 'set a prudent budget' and 'promptly review new information'.
findings.matters: A 15%+ funding reduction in year three of this five-year strategy, with no identified mitigation, represents a material and unresolved fiscal pressure. This creates uncertainty about the council's financial sustainability beyond 2029/30.

findings.headline: Business Rates Reset has reduced retained income by £7.6m, shifting funding dependency to government grants.

The shift represents a structural change from locally-raised revenue to grant dependency.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand how councils are funded and whether that funding is stable or volatile. A 37% reduction in retained business rates and shift to grant dependency creates reliance on central government decisions, which are subject to political change.

findings.matters: Reliance on asset sales is finite; when disposal opportunities exhaust or asset valuations decline, the capital programme faces a cliff, suggesting the council lacks sufficient revenue capacity to fund capital renewal from operations
